messages.author: 55d1a09c85eadab7
messages.subject: Requests for Stan in Japan
parts:
Hi,

I'd like to share a blog post as @mcmc_stan suggested.

Many thanks,
Bee
----
I asked Stan lecture's attendees what they wanted as a new feature at the registration, and summarized the 60+ answers. Here is the result:

[fig.png]

"experience" means experience of Stan: 1 = Never, 2 = several models, 3 = 20+ models. We can say there are 2 major requests, "speed-up" and "discrete parameters".

- "speed-up" includes GPU, online learning and distributed processing
- "more ADVI" includes clarifying/increasing applicable models and PyStan support
- "information criteria" includes calculation of WAIC/WBIC within Stan

Most attendees (including me) often give up using NUTS due to the amount of data. Therefore, "speed-up" is desired eagerly. It seems to be possible to split a huge dataset into rows and calculate differentiation by row in parallel, then merge them. Certainly it is difficult to retain cross-platform with GPU, but I think cross-platform is not very important these days, because we can choose any OS at cloud. I'd like to pick up backward compatibility. I hope Stan 3 would retain "backward compatibility" on sampling statement "~".

Thus an end-users questionnaire could be good information. Perhaps it should be done for a larger scale. We would appreciate it if this post could be a hint for Stan team members to consider the priorities of new features.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Requests for Stan in Japan
parts:
Thanks. I'm not sure who was writing as @mcmc_stan.

Efficiency and scalability are often conflated, but they
are usually separate concerns. For example, if your
algorithm takes a lot of memory per data item and runs
on a single CPU, it's not going to scale no matter how
fast it is.

What often happens is that efficiency is the bottleneck
to running bigger models rather than scalablity per se.
That is, the model would fit given lots of time, just
not efficiently enough. MCMC in general and Stan
in particular have problems with both.

Speedup and scaling comes in many forms. We could run
on GPUs, which would definitely give us more speed, but
we might not be able to scale really well because of the
size of the derivative graph if we try to keep the entire
density expression graph in memory.

We could spend more time developing distributed
algorithms, which would let us scale out. That's really
the only way to get true large-scale scalability.

We could also distribute with multi-threading, but that's
more likely to be an efficiency gain than a scalability gain.

Stochastic methods (like online variational inference) could
give us both speed and scalability.

We're certainly open to suggestions on what people want
implemented. I don't think we'll be doing DIC or AIC
or BIC---we'll probably stick to the recommendations of the
LOO package.

The Rstudio people have added some neat Stan functionality.

Not sure what people want for copulas.

Discrete parameters are an issue with the modeling language.
We can't compute the Markov blanket you can compute with
a graphical model, so we can't easily compute conditionals.
We might put a graphical model wrapper layer on top of Stan,
at which point, conditionals will be possible.

- Bob

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Requests for Stan in Japan
parts:
Hi Bee,

@mcmc_stan is me.

I was hoping you'd put up the link to the blog-post. There was a lot of narrative there that I wanted to address, but it looks like it was pulled down. If you still have the text, it'd be good to address those points directly. 

Regarding GPUs, I'm not convinced they'd help for most Stan programs. The way Stan works, things just aren't easily parallelized. We could offload Eigen computations to GPU. We just need some expertise to help build Stan so it can leverage that. If you or anyone has GPU programming skills, we'd love to see a prototype. Even if it ends up being slower.

We'd love to have more interaction with the communities that are out there using Stan. If there are very specific things we can fix and fix easily, it would be good to add issues on our issue trackers. If they are open-ended research problems, talk to us if you're interested in tackling them.



Daniel

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Requests for Stan in Japan
parts:
The pseudo-code for NUTS is in the Hoffman and Gelman
NUTS paper. Just be careful to use the second (efficient)
version. It's just pseudo-code, not Julia.

We should definitely write up the higher-level
organization of the C++ code. We'll probably do that
after the dust settles on the services refactor and
we pull out a couple more repositories for the language
and for the algorithms.

The longer-term to-do list Wiki is the closest we have
to a map. What we're lacking is a planned route through
it or any estimated times of arrival in various locations.

We're trying to write case studies on best practices for
modeling. And put together a couple books. All of these
will be more tutorial in nature than the manual. I'm also
going to split out the reference manual part of the manual
when I get a chance and tighten up the language "spec" there.

- Bob
